claim: Mouse–rat chimeras were viable.

claim: Mouse–rat chimeras were smaller than age-matched rats.
source: While mouse–rat chimeras were viable, they were smaller than age-matched rats (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by photographs in Figure 1B and weight measurements in Figure 1C

claim: Mixed black and white pigmentation distinguished the mouse–rat chimeras from juvenile rats.
source: Consistent with the presence of mouse ESC-derived cells (black) in the skin tissue (Wang et al., 2021), mixed black and white pigmentation distinguished the mouse–rat chimeras from juvenile rats (Figure 1B).

claim: The average body weight of mouse–rat chimeras was smaller than rats, but larger than mice of similar age.
source: The average body weight of mouse–rat chimeras was smaller than rats, but larger than mice of similar age (Figure 1C).

claim: ESC-derived cells were abundant in femur and tibia bones of the chimeras as evidenced by GFP fluorescence.
source: ESC-derived cells were abundant in femur and tibia bones of the chimeras as evidenced by GFP fluorescence (Figure 1D).

claim: The percentage of ESC-derived cells in BM of juvenile mouse–rat chimeras was 15–50%.
source: FACS analysis of BM cells obtained from juvenile mouse–rat chimeras revealed that the percentage of ESC-derived cells was 15–50% (Figure 1E, F).
evidence: Supported by FACS analysis data shown in Figure 1E and 1F

claim: The percentage of LSKs was higher in the BM of mouse–rat chimeras compared to the control.
source: The percentage of LSKs was higher in the BM of mouse–rat chimeras compared to the control (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by FACS analysis data shown in Figure 1G

claim: The percentage of LT-HSCs among LSKs was higher in mouse–rat chimeras.

claim: Total numbers of HSCs (LT-HSCs + ST-HSCs) were higher in mouse–rat chimeras compared to mice of the same age.

claim: Mouse ESCs can differentiate into hematopoietic progenitor cells in the BM of mouse–rat chimeras.
source: Thus, mouse ESCs can differentiate into hematopoietic progenitor cells in the BM of mouse–rat chimeras.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from FACS analysis data showing presence of HSCs and other progenitors

claim: 11,326 cells from 14 major cell subtypes were identified in the combined BM datasets from mouse–mouse and mouse–rat chimeras.
source: Based on published gene expression signatures of mouse BM cells (Baccin et al., 2020), 11,326 cells from 14 major cell subtypes were identified: 5308 cells from control mouse–mouse chimeras and 6018 cells from mouse–rat chimeras.

claim: The 14 major cell subtypes identified include lymphoid, erythroid, myeloid, and neutrophil progenitors, Pro-B, Pre-B, B and T lymphocytes, megakaryocytes, dendritic cells, neutrophils, basophils/eosinophils, monocytes, and LMPP cells.
source: These include lymphoid, erythroid, myeloid, and neutrophil progenitors, Pro-B, Pre-B, B and T lymphocytes, megakaryocytes, dendritic cells, neutrophils, basophils/eosinophils, monocytes, and LMPP cells (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by UMAP clustering analysis shown in Figure 2A

claim: Analysis of BM cells from mouse–rat and mouse–mouse chimeras demonstrated similar distributions of hematopoietic cell lineages derived from CMP and CLP.
source: Analysis of BM cells from mouse–rat and mouse–mouse chimeras demonstrated similar distributions of hematopoietic cell lineages derived from CMP and CLP (Figure 2A), indicating identical cell types in mouse–rat and control chimeras.
evidence: Supported by UMAP analysis shown in Figure 2A

claim: Percentages of CLP-derived lymphoid progenitors, Pro-B, Pre-B, and B cells were lower in mouse–rat chimeras compared to the control.
source: Percentages CLP-derived lymphoid progenitors, Pro-B, Pre-B, and B cells were lower in mouse–rat chimeras compared to the control (Figure 2A, B).
evidence: Supported by cell cluster percentages shown in Figure 2B

claim: Percentages of CMP-derived erythroid, myeloid and neutrophil progenitors, dendritic cells, and basophils/eosinophils were higher in mouse–rat chimeras.
source: In contrast, percentages of CMP-derived erythroid, myeloid and neutrophil progenitors, dendritic cells, and basophils/eosinophils were higher (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by cell cluster percentages shown in Figure 2B

claim: Monocytes and neutrophils were similar between mouse–rat chimeras and controls.
source: Monocytes and neutrophils were similar, whereas megakaryocytes were decreased in the BM of mouse–rat chimeras (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by cell cluster percentages shown in Figure 2B

claim: Megakaryocytes were decreased in the BM of mouse–rat chimeras.
source: Monocytes and neutrophils were similar, whereas megakaryocytes were decreased in the BM of mouse–rat chimeras (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by cell cluster percentages shown in Figure 2B

claim: The percentage of LMPPs in mouse–rat chimeras was increased compared to the control.
source: The percentage of LMPPs in mouse–rat chimeras was increased compared to the control (Figure 2A, B).
evidence: Supported by cell cluster percentages shown in Figure 2B

claim: HSCs were identified by coexpression of Kit, Ly6a(Sca1), and Flt3 mRNAs.
source: HSCs, identified by coexpression of Kit, Ly6a(Sca1), and Flt3 mRNAs (Rowe et al., 2016; Vo and Daley, 2015), clustered together with myeloid and erythroid progenitors (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A, B).
evidence: Supported by gene expression analysis and citations to published methods

claim: The number of ESC-derived HSCs was higher in BM of mouse–rat chimeras compared to the control.
source: The number of ESC-derived HSCs was higher in BM of mouse–rat chimeras compared to the control (Figure 2—figure supplement 4C), findings consistent with FACS analysis (Figure 1H, I).
evidence: Supported by single-cell RNA sequencing data and FACS analysis

claim: Only 6 out of 6018 BM cells (0.1%) in mouse–rat chimeras contained both mouse and rat mRNA transcripts.
source: Only 6 out of 6018 BM cells (0.1%) in mouse–rat chimeras contained both mouse and rat mRNA transcripts (Supplementary files 1 and 2), indicating that the fusion of mouse and rat BM cells is rare.
evidence: Supported by single-cell RNA sequencing data analysis

claim: The fusion of mouse and rat BM cells is rare.
source: Only 6 out of 6018 BM cells (0.1%) in mouse–rat chimeras contained both mouse and rat mRNA transcripts (Supplementary files 1 and 2), indicating that the fusion of mouse and rat BM cells is rare.
evidence: Inferred from the low percentage of cells containing both mouse and rat transcripts

claim: Gene expression signatures of ESC-derived hematopoietic cells were similar in mouse–rat and control mouse–mouse chimeras.
source: Thus, gene expression signatures of ESC-derived hematopoietic cells were similar in mouse–rat and control mouse–mouse chimeras.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from correlation analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplements 5B and 6B

claim: Mouse cells preferentially contributed to hematopoietic progenitors and endothelial cells in chimeric BM.
source: Thus, mouse cells preferentially contributed to hematopoietic progenitors and endothelial cells, whereas rat cells contributed to the majority of chondrocytes and fibroblasts.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from cell cluster analysis shown in Figure 3A and 3B

claim: Rat cells contributed to the majority of chondrocytes and fibroblasts in chimeric BM.
source: Thus, mouse cells preferentially contributed to hematopoietic progenitors and endothelial cells, whereas rat cells contributed to the majority of chondrocytes and fibroblasts.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from cell cluster analysis shown in Figure 3A and 3B

claim: Endothelial cells interacted with EMPs through the Cxcl12-Cxcr4 receptor–ligand signaling pair.
source: Regardless of mouse and rat origins of BM cells, endothelial cells interacted with EMPs through the Cxcl12-Cxcr4 receptor–ligand signaling pair.
evidence: Supported by ligand-receptor interaction analysis shown in Figure 4

claim: The main signaling circuit between fibroblasts and EMPs was Lama2-Itga6.
source: The main signaling circuit between fibroblasts and EMPs was Lama2-Itga6, whereas chondrocytes signaled to EMPs through App-Itga6 and Comp-Cd47 pathways (Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by ligand-receptor interaction analysis shown in Figure 4

claim: Chondrocytes signaled to EMPs through App-Itga6 and Comp-Cd47 pathways.
source: The main signaling circuit between fibroblasts and EMPs was Lama2-Itga6, whereas chondrocytes signaled to EMPs through App-Itga6 and Comp-Cd47 pathways (Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by ligand-receptor interaction analysis shown in Figure 4

claim: Major receptor–ligand interactions between GMP cells and stromal cells include Cxcl12-Cxcr4 signaling between endothelial cells and GMPs.
source: Major receptor–ligand interactions between granulocyte–monocyte progenitor (GMP) cells and stromal cells were also similar in BM cells of mouse and rat origin (Figure 4—figure supplement 1). These include Cxcl12-Cxcr4 signaling between endothelial cells and GMPs, Col1a1-Cd44 signaling between fibroblasts and GMPs, and App-Il18rap signaling between chondrocytes and GMPs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by ligand-receptor interaction analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: Col1a1-Cd44 signaling occurs between fibroblasts and GMPs.
source: These include Cxcl12-Cxcr4 signaling between endothelial cells and GMPs, Col1a1-Cd44 signaling between fibroblasts and GMPs, and App-Il18rap signaling between chondrocytes and GMPs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by ligand-receptor interaction analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: App-Il18rap signaling occurs between chondrocytes and GMPs.
source: These include Cxcl12-Cxcr4 signaling between endothelial cells and GMPs, Col1a1-Cd44 signaling between fibroblasts and GMPs, and App-Il18rap signaling between chondrocytes and GMPs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by ligand-receptor interaction analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: Mouse and rat BM cells use similar signaling pathways between stromal and hematopoietic progenitor cells.
source: These results demonstrate that mouse and rat BM cells use similar signaling pathways between stromal and hematopoietic progenitor cells.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from ligand-receptor interaction analysis

claim: Mouse embryos were significantly larger than rat and mouse–rat chimeric embryos at E11.
source: At E11, mouse embryos were significantly larger than rat and mouse–rat chimeric embryos (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), consistent with previous studies demonstrating that the main stages of mouse embryonic development occur approximately 1.5 days faster compared to embryonic development in the rat (Farrington-Rock et al., 2008; Marcela et al., 2012; Takahashi and Osumi, 2005; Torres et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by embryo size comparison images and citations to published studies

claim: The main stages of mouse embryonic development occur approximately 1.5 days faster compared to embryonic development in the rat.
source: At E11, mouse embryos were significantly larger than rat and mouse–rat chimeric embryos (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), consistent with previous studies demonstrating that the main stages of mouse embryonic development occur approximately 1.5 days faster compared to embryonic development in the rat (Farrington-Rock et al., 2008; Marcela et al., 2012; Takahashi and Osumi, 2005; Torres et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies

claim: In the dorsal aorta of mouse–rat chimeras, the majority of FLK1+RUNX1+ cells expressed GFP, indicating the mouse origin of these cells.
source: In the dorsal aorta of mouse–rat chimeras, the majority of FLK1+RUNX1+ cells expressed GFP, indicating the mouse origin of these cells (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining images shown in Figure 5B

claim: Percentages of mouse Lin− cells, LSKs, and ST-HSCs were higher in fetal livers of mouse–rat chimeras.
source: Later in development, percentages of mouse Lin− cells, LSKs, and ST-HSCs were higher in fetal livers of mouse–rat chimeras as demonstrated by FACS analysis for Lin, CD117, Sca1, CD48, and CD150 (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by FACS analysis data shown in Figure 5C

claim: The percentage of LT-HSC in fetal livers was unchanged between mouse–rat chimeras and controls.
source: The percentage of LT-HSC in fetal livers was unchanged (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by FACS analysis data shown in Figure 5C

claim: ESC complementation causes the earlier development of donor HSCs in the dorsal aorta.
source: Thus, ESC complementation causes the earlier development of donor HSCs in the dorsal aorta and increases percentages of donor-derived Lin− cells, LSKs, and ST-HSCs in the fetal liver.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from immunostaining and FACS analysis data

claim: ESC complementation increases percentages of donor-derived Lin− cells, LSKs, and ST-HSCs in the fetal liver.
source: Thus, ESC complementation causes the earlier development of donor HSCs in the dorsal aorta and increases percentages of donor-derived Lin− cells, LSKs, and ST-HSCs in the fetal liver.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from FACS analysis data shown in Figure 5C

claim: All mice without BM transplant died between 9 and 12 days after irradiation.
source: Consistent with published studies (Rowe et al., 2016; Sugimura et al., 2017; Vo and Daley, 2015), all mice without BM transplant died between 9 and 12 days after irradiation (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by survival analysis shown in Figure 6B and citations to published studies

claim: All 20 mice transplanted with GFP+ BM cells from mouse–rat chimeras survived after lethal irradiation.
source: In contrast, all 20 mice transplanted with GFP+ BM cells from mouse–rat chimeras survived after lethal irradiation (Figure 6B, C).
evidence: Supported by survival analysis shown in Figure 6B

claim: Transplantation of ESC-derived BM cells from mouse–rat chimeras increased WBC and the numbers of granulocytes, monocytes, and lymphocytes in the peripheral blood at day 8.
source: Transplantation of ESC-derived BM cells from mouse–rat chimeras increased WBC and the numbers of granulocytes, monocytes, and lymphocytes in the peripheral blood at day 8 (Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: Supported by blood analysis data shown in Figure 7A

claim: Contribution of ESC-derived BM cells to granulocytes, monocytes, and B cells was higher compared to erythroid and T cells at day 8.
source: Contribution of ESC-derived BM cells to granulocytes, monocytes, and B cells was higher compared to erythroid and T cells (Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by FACS analysis data shown in Figure 7B

claim: At 5 months after BM transplantation, ESC-derived cells completely restored blood cell numbers, PLT and Hb in lethally irradiated mice.
source: At 5 months after BM transplantation, ESC-derived cells completely restored blood cell numbers, PLT and Hb in lethally irradiated mice (Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: Supported by blood analysis data shown in Figure 7C

claim: Long-term contributions of ESC-derived BM cells to all hematopoietic cell lineages in the peripheral blood were between 49% and 96%.
source: Long-term contributions of ESC-derived BM cells to all hematopoietic cell lineages in the peripheral blood were between 49% and 96% (Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by FACS analysis data shown in Figure 7C

claim: Transplantation of ESC-derived BM cells from mouse–rat chimeras prevented mortality and restored hematopoietic blood lineages in lethally irradiated syngeneic mice.
source: Thus, transplantation of ESC-derived BM cells from mouse–rat chimeras prevented mortality and restored hematopoietic blood lineages in lethally irradiated syngeneic mice.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from survival and blood analysis data

claim: Transplantation of ESC-derived BM cells significantly increased LSKs but did not affect the numbers of ST-HSCs and LT-HSCs in irradiated mice at day 8.
source: Transplantation of ESC-derived BM cells significantly increased LSKs but did not affect the numbers of ST-HSCs and LT-HSCs in irradiated mice (Figure 7D).
evidence: Supported by FACS analysis data shown in Figure 7D

claim: Contribution of ESC-derived BM cells to Lin− and LSK cell subsets was high at day 8.
source: Contribution of ESC-derived BM cells to Lin− and LSK cell subsets was high, whereas ESC contribution to ST-HSCs and LT-HSCs at day 8 was low (Figure 7E and Figure 7—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Supported by FACS analysis data shown in Figure 7E

claim: ESC contribution to ST-HSCs and LT-HSCs at day 8 was low.
source: Contribution of ESC-derived BM cells to Lin− and LSK cell subsets was high, whereas ESC contribution to ST-HSCs and LT-HSCs at day 8 was low (Figure 7E and Figure 7—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Supported by FACS analysis data shown in Figure 7E

claim: At 5 months after BM transplantation, percentages of LSKs, ST-HSCs, and LT-HSCs in the BM were increased.
source: At 5 months after BM transplantation, percentages of LSKs, ST-HSCs, and LT-HSCs in the BM were increased (Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: Supported by FACS analysis data shown in Figure 7D

claim: Long-term contribution of ESC-derived BM cells to LSKs, ST-HSCs, and LT-HSCs was between 92% and 95%.
source: Long-term contribution of ESC-derived BM cells to LSKs, ST-HSCs, and LT-HSCs was between 92% and 95% (Figure 7F and Figure 7—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Supported by FACS analysis data shown in Figure 7F

claim: The secondary BM transplantation rescued lethally irradiated mice and resulted in long-term engraftment of ESC-derived HSCs into hematopoietic cell lineages in the BM and peripheral blood.
source: The secondary BM transplantation rescued lethally irradiated mice and resulted in long-term engraftment of ESC-derived HSCs into hematopoietic cell lineages in the BM and peripheral blood (Figure 7—figure supplement 6B–E).
evidence: Supported by survival and FACS analysis data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 6

claim: Transplantation of ESC-derived BM cells from mouse–rat chimeras resulted in efficient, long-term contribution of donor cells to the BM and blood of lethally irradiated mice.
source: Altogether, transplantation of ESC-derived BM cells from mouse–rat chimeras resulted in efficient, long-term contribution of donor cells to the BM and blood of lethally irradiated mice.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from transplantation experiments and FACS analysis data

claim: Interspecies mouse–rat chimeras were viable and contained approximately 25% of ESC-derived mouse cells in the BM.
source: Interspecies mouse–rat chimeras were viable and contained approximately 25% of ESC-derived mouse cells in the BM.
evidence: Supported by FACS analysis data showing 15-50% ESC-derived cells

claim: ESCs contributed to all hematopoietic cell lineages in interspecies BM.
source: While ESCs contributed to all hematopoietic cell lineages in interspecies BM, the percentage of lymphoid progenitors was lower, whereas the percentages of myeloid progenitor cells and HSCs were higher in mouse–rat chimeras compared to control mouse–mouse chimeras.
evidence: Supported by single-cell RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 2

claim: Chimeric HSCs develop more efficiently from donor mouse cells in the dorsal aorta, fetal liver, and BM, whereas rat cells are less efficient to differentiate into HSCs.
source: Our data demonstrate that chimeric HSCs develop more efficiently from donor mouse cells in the dorsal aorta, fetal liver, and BM, whereas rat cells are less efficient to differentiate into HSCs.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from immunostaining and FACS analysis data shown in Figure 5

claim: Using donor ESCs from species with less gestational time in interspecies 'bioreactors' can lead to larger quantities of ESC-derived hematopoietic progenitors in the chimeric BM.
source: These data suggest that using donor ESCs from species with less gestational time in interspecies 'bioreactors' can lead to larger quantities of ESC-derived hematopoietic progenitors in the chimeric BM.
evidence: Speculative conclusion based on observed differences in developmental timing

claim: Cxcl12-Cxcr4 signaling between hematopoietic progenitors and endothelial cells plays a critical role in maintenance of HSCs during BM homeostasis and promotes niche regeneration and hematopoietic reconstitution after BM transplantation.
source: These pathways include Cxcl12-Cxcr4 signaling between hematopoietic progenitors and endothelial cells, which plays a critical role in maintenance of HSCs during BM homeostasis and promotes niche regeneration and hematopoietic reconstitution after BM transplantation (Baccin et al., 2020; Singh et al., 2020; Sugiyama et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies

claim: Mouse ESC-derived cells from multiple hematopoietic cell lineages were indistinguishable from normal mouse BM cells based on gene expression signatures and cell surface proteins.
source: Despite mosaicism in interspecies BM, mouse ESC-derived cells from multiple hematopoietic cell lineages were highly differentiated and indistinguishable from the normal mouse BM cells based on gene expression signatures and cell surface proteins.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from single-cell RNA sequencing and FACS analysis data

claim: Transplantation of BM cells into lethally irradiated syngeneic mice prevented mortality and resulted in long-term contribution of ESC-derived cells to all hematopoietic cell lineages in the BM and peripheral blood.
source: Consistent with functional competency of ESC-derived BM, transplantation of BM cells into lethally irradiated syngeneic mice prevented mortality and resulted in long-term contribution of ESC-derived cells to all hematopoietic cell lineages in the BM and peripheral blood.
evidence: Supported by survival and FACS analysis data shown in Figures 6 and 7

claim: Long-term contribution of donor BM cells to ST-HSCs and LT-HSCs of irradiated mice was high, supporting the ability of donor HSCs to self-renew.
source: Interestingly, long-term contribution of donor BM cells to ST-HSCs and LT-HSCs of irradiated mice was high, supporting the ability of donor HSCs to self-renew.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from FACS analysis data shown in Figure 7F

claim: Low contribution of donor BM to HSCs at day 8 is consistent with an acute hematopoietic deficiency in lethally irradiated mice.
source: Low contribution of donor BM to HSCs at day 8 is not surprising considering an acute hematopoietic deficiency in lethally irradiated mice.
evidence: Inference based on understanding of hematopoietic response to irradiation

claim: Most donor-derived HSCs undergo rapid differentiation into other hematopoietic cell types to compensate for the loss of injured hematopoietic cells after irradiation.
source: It is possible that most donor-derived HSCs undergo rapid differentiation into other hematopoietic cell types to compensate for the loss of injured hematopoietic cells after irradiation.
evidence: Speculative explanation for low HSC contribution at day 8

claim: Interspecies chimeras could be considered for in vivo differentiation of patient-derived iPSCs into hematopoietic cell lineages for future cell therapies.
source: Thus, the interspecies chimeras could be considered for in vivo differentiation of patient-derived iPSCs into hematopoietic cell lineages for future cell therapies.
evidence: Speculative conclusion about potential therapeutic applications

claim: A fully functional BM was generated from mouse ESCs using rat embryos as 'bioreactors'.
source: Altogether, a fully functional BM was generated from mouse ESCs using rat embryos as 'bioreactors'.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from all experimental data including transplantation studies

claim: The BM is a remarkably complex organ consisting of multiple mesenchymal, immune, endothelial, and neuronal cell types which together comprise a highly specialized microenvironment required to support blood regeneration or hematopoiesis.
source: The bone marrow (BM) is a remarkably complex organ consisting of multiple mesenchymal, immune, endothelial, and neuronal cell types which together comprise a highly specialized microenvironment required to support c blood regeneration or hematopoiesis (Baccin et al., 2020; Baryawno et al., 2019; Rowe et al., 2016; Tikhonova et al., 2019; Vo and Daley, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies

claim: Hematopoiesis occurs in a stepwise manner and is initiated by a heterogeneous, multipotent, population of hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs), located at the apex of the hematopoietic differentiation tree.
source: Hematopoiesis occurs in a stepwise manner and is initiated by a heterogeneous, multipotent, population of hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs), located at the apex of the hematopoietic differentiation tree.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about hematopoiesis

claim: Long-term HSCs (LT-HSCs) remain quiescent to maintain their undifferentiated state within the BM niche.
source: Long-term HSCs (LT-HSCs) remain quiescent to maintain their undifferentiated state within the BM niche.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about HSC biology

claim: LT-HSCs can either undergo differentiation or self-renewal, to maintain the HSC pool.
source: When necessary, LT-HSCs can either undergo differentiation or self-renewal, to maintain the HSC pool.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about HSC biology

claim: Short-term HSCs (ST-HSCs) are restricted in their self-renewal capacity and primed for differentiation into multipotent progenitors (MPPs).
source: Conversely, short-term HSCs (ST-HSCs) are restricted in their self-renewal capacity and primed for differentiation into multipotent progenitors (MPPs), initiating the process of blood cell development.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about HSC biology

claim: MPPs further differentiate into common myeloid progenitors (CMPs), lymphoid-primed multipotent progenitors (LMPPs), and common lymphoid progenitors (CLPs) that become increasingly lineage restricted with subsequent cell divisions, ultimately yielding all mature blood cell types.
source: MPPs further differentiate into common myeloid progenitors (CMPs), lymphoid-primed multipotent progenitors (LMPPs), and common lymphoid progenitors (CLPs) that become increasingly lineage restricted with subsequent cell divisions, ultimately yielding all mature blood cell types (Haas et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to published study

claim: The most biologically relevant way to test HSC function remains to be through serial transplantation and hematopoietic reconstitution of irradiated recipient mice.
source: Classically, the most biologically relevant way to test HSC function remains to be through serial transplantation and hematopoietic reconstitution of irradiated recipient mice (Purton and Scadden, 2007; Rowe et al., 2016; Vo and Daley, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies

claim: Generation of functional BM from embryonic stem cells (ESCs) or induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) promises to provide new therapeutic opportunities for hematologic and autoimmune disorders.
source: Generation of functional BM from embryonic stem cells (ESCs) or induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) promises to provide new therapeutic opportunities for hematologic and autoimmune disorders.
evidence: Statement about potential therapeutic applications

claim: This approach is limited by technical challenges to produce functional HSCs or the mixture of hematopoietic progenitors capable of replacing all mature blood cell types after cell transplantation.
source: However, this approach is limited by technical challenges to produce functional HSCs or the mixture of hematopoietic progenitors capable of replacing all mature blood cell types after cell transplantation.
evidence: Statement about current limitations in the field

claim: HSC-like cells have been generated from mouse and human ESCs and iPSCs using in vitro differentiation protocols.
source: HSC-like cells have been generated from mouse and human ESCs and iPSCs using in vitro differentiation protocols (Amabile et al., 2013; Doulatov et al., 2013; Grigoriadis et al., 2010; Kitajima et al., 2011; Ledran et al., 2008; Sugimura et al., 2017; Vodyanik et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies

claim: ESCs and iPSCs have been used to produce myeloid and lymphoid progenitor cells as well as differentiated hematopoietic cells, including neutrophils, monocytes, erythroid cells, and T and B lymphocytes.
source: Likewise, ESCs and iPSCs have been used to produce myeloid and lymphoid progenitor cells as well as differentiated hematopoietic cells, including neutrophils, monocytes, erythroid cells, and T and B lymphocytes (Doulatov et al., 2013; Elcheva et al., 2014; Galic et al., 2006; Kennedy et al., 2012; Montel-Hagen et al., 2019; Nafria et al., 2020; Vodyanik et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies

claim: When transplanted into irradiated animals, ESC/iPSC-derived hematopoietic progenitor cells undergo differentiation and engraft into the BM niche, providing an important source of renewal and regeneration for various blood cell lineages.
source: When transplanted into irradiated animals, ESC/iPSC-derived hematopoietic progenitor cells undergo differentiation and engraft into the BM niche, providing an important source of renewal and regeneration for various blood cell lineages (Rowe et al., 2016; Sugimura et al., 2017; Vo and Daley, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies

claim: ESC/iPSC-derived hematopoietic cells often express appropriate cell markers, but gene expression and functional studies indicate significant differences between ESC/iPSC-derived cells and endogenous cells that have undergone normal morphogenesis in the BM.
source: While ESC/iPSC-derived hematopoietic cells often express appropriate cell markers, gene expression and functional studies indicate significant differences between ESC/iPSC-derived cells and endogenous cells that have undergone normal morphogenesis in the BM (Lin et al., 2019; Lu et al., 2016; Sugimura et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies

claim: In vivo differentiation of ESCs into multiple cell lineages can be achieved using blastocyst complementation, in which donor ESCs are injected into blastocysts of recipient animals to create chimeras.
source: In vivo differentiation of ESCs into multiple cell lineages can be achieved using blastocyst complementation, in which donor ESCs are injected into blastocysts of recipient animals to create chimeras.
evidence: Statement about established methodology

claim: Fluorescently labeled ESCs undergo differentiation in recipient embryos that serve as 'biological reactors' by providing growth factors, hormones, and cellular niches to support ESC differentiation in the embryo.
source: Fluorescently labeled ESCs undergo differentiation in recipient embryos that serve as 'biological reactors' by providing growth factors, hormones, and cellular niches to support ESC differentiation in the embryo.
evidence: Statement about the mechanism of blastocyst complementation

claim: In mouse and rat apancreatic Pdx1−/− embryos, donor ESCs formed an entire pancreas in which both exocrine and endocrine cells were almost entirely derived from ESCs or iPSCs.
source: In mouse and rat apancreatic Pdx1−/− embryos, donor ESCs formed an entire pancreas in which both exocrine and endocrine cells were almost entirely derived from ESCs or iPSCs (Kobayashi et al., 2010; Yamaguchi et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies

claim: Mouse ESC/iPSC-derived β-cells from mouse–rat chimeras were fully differentiated and successfully rescued syngeneic diabetic mice.
source: Mouse ESC/iPSC-derived β-cells from mouse–rat chimeras were fully differentiated and successfully rescued syngeneic diabetic mice (Yamaguchi et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to published study

claim: ESCs generated pancreatic cell lineages in apancreatic pigs.
source: ESCs generated pancreatic cell lineages in apancreatic pigs (Matsunari et al., 2013), kidney in Sall1-deficient rats (Goto et al., 2019), endothelial cells in Flk1−/− mice (Hamanaka et al., 2018), lymphocytes in immunodeficient mice (Muthusamy et al., 2011), and neuronal progenitors in mice with forebrain-specific overexpression of diphtheria toxin (Chang et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies

claim: Mouse ESCs were used to generate lung and thyroid tissues in embryos deficient for Fgf10, Nkx2-1, Fgfr2, or β-catenin.
source: Recently, mouse ESCs were used to generate lung and thyroid tissues in embryos deficient for Fgf10, Nkx2-1, Fgfr2, or β-catenin (Kitahara et al., 2020; Mori et al., 2019; Wen et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies

claim: Mouse ESCs effectively produced hematopoietic cells in mice deficient for Kit or Flk1 using blastocyst complementation.
source: Using blastocyst complementation, mouse ESCs effectively produced hematopoietic cells in mice deficient for Kit or Flk1 (Hamanaka et al., 2018; Jansson and Larsson, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies

claim: ESC-derived endothelial progenitor cells from mouse–rat chimeras were indistinguishable from endogenous endothelial progenitor cells based on gene expression signatures and functional properties.
source: ESC-derived endothelial progenitor cells from mouse–rat chimeras were indistinguishable from endogenous endothelial progenitor cells based on gene expression signatures and functional properties (Wang et al., 2021), indicating that ESC/iPSC-derived progenitors can be used for tissue regeneration (Bolte et al., 2020a; Bolte et al., 2018; Dharmadhikari et al., 2015; Kolesnichenko et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies

claim: Generation of functional BM from ESCs in interspecies chimeras has not yet been achieved prior to this study.
source: While all these studies support the effectiveness of blastocyst complementation for differentiation of multiple cell types from ESCs/iPSCs in vivo, generation of functional BM from ESCs in interspecies chimeras has not yet been achieved.
evidence: Statement about the novelty of the current study
